chapter.name: Statistics
chapter.blurb: A school's own marks, a hospital's patient ages, a city's household expenditures -- once real data is grouped into class intervals for convenience, the exact value of any single observation is lost, yet a single representative number can still be recovered for the whole distribution. This chapter extends the three measures of central tendency already met for ungrouped data -- mean, median and mode -- to grouped data: the mean by three equivalent routes (direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation), the mode by locating the modal class and adjusting for its neighbours' frequencies, and the median by building a cumulative frequency table and finding the one class where the running total crosses halfway. A closing section compares the three measures for different practical questions and gives an approximate empirical relationship linking them.

concepts.name: Mean of Grouped Data: the Direct Method
concepts.description: Finding the mean of grouped data by treating every observation in a class as if located at that class's mid-point (class mark), then applying mean = (sum of f_i * x_i) / (sum of f_i).
concepts.idea: The mean of grouped data is found by treating every observation in a class as if it were located at that class's mid-point (class mark), then applying the same sum-of-values-over-count idea used for ungrouped data.
concepts.rule: Class mark x_i = (upper class limit + lower class limit) / 2 for each class. Then mean = (sum of f_i * x_i) / (sum of f_i), summed over all classes. This is the Direct Method.

concepts.name: Mean of Grouped Data: Assumed-Mean and Step-Deviation Methods
concepts.description: Finding the mean of grouped data by subtracting a fixed assumed mean 'a' from every class mark (and, in the step-deviation method, dividing by the class size h) to simplify the arithmetic, then correcting back to give the same mean as the direct method.
concepts.idea: Subtracting a fixed assumed mean 'a' from every class mark turns large numbers into small deviations, making the arithmetic easier while giving exactly the same mean as the direct method.
concepts.rule: Assumed-mean method: d_i = x_i - a; mean = a + (sum of f_i * d_i) / (sum of f_i). Step-deviation method: u_i = (x_i - a) / h, where h is the class size; mean = a + h * (sum of f_i * u_i) / (sum of f_i). All three methods (direct, assumed-mean, step-deviation) always give the same mean; step-deviation is most convenient when the d_i's share a common factor.
concepts.example: For class marks 17.5, 32.5, 47.5, 62.5, 77.5, 92.5 (frequencies 2, 3, 7, 6, 6, 6), taking a = 47.5 and h = 15: sum of f_i * d_i = 435 gives mean = 47.5 + 435/30 = 62; sum of f_i * u_i = 29 gives mean = 47.5 + 15 * (29/30) = 62 -- matching the direct method's mean of 62 exactly (p. 175-177).

questions.a: Algebraically, d_i = x_i - a and u_i = d_i / h are just linear rescalings of x_i; when substituted back into the mean formula (a + (sum of f_i * d_i)/(sum of f_i), or a + h times the u_i version), the a's and h's cancel out exactly, giving the same result as (sum of f_i * x_i)/(sum of f_i). Explains that these transformations algebraically cancel out in the mean formula, giving the same result as the direct method

concepts.name: Mode of Grouped Data
concepts.description: Locating the modal class (the class of highest frequency) in a grouped distribution, then applying the mode formula using the modal class's lower limit, class size, and the frequencies of the modal class and its two neighbours.
concepts.idea: The mode of grouped data is not read directly from frequencies as in ungrouped data; instead, you first locate the modal class (the class with the highest frequency), then use a formula that adjusts the modal class's lower limit toward whichever neighbouring class has more competing frequency.
concepts.rule: Mode = l + ((f_1 - f_0) / (2*f_1 - f_0 - f_2)) * h, where l = lower limit of the modal class, h = class size, f_1 = frequency of the modal class, f_0 = frequency of the class preceding the modal class, f_2 = frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.
concepts.example: For family-size data with classes 1-3, 3-5, 5-7, 7-9, 9-11 and frequencies 7, 8, 2, 2, 1, the modal class is 3-5 (highest frequency, 8); l=3, h=2, f_1=8, f_0=7, f_2=2, giving mode = 3 + ((8-7)/(16-7-2)) * 2 = 3 + 2/7 = 3.286 (p. 184-185).

questions.a: For grouped data, an entire class of values (not a single value) has the highest frequency, so we only know that the mode lies somewhere inside that class (the modal class); the mode formula is needed to locate one specific value inside that class, using the neighbouring classes' frequencies, since naming the class alone is not a single number.

concepts.name: Cumulative Frequency Distributions and the Median Class
concepts.description: Building a running (cumulative) total of class frequencies, either upward from the lowest class (less than type) or downward from the highest class (more than type), and comparing it against half the total number of observations to locate the median class.
concepts.idea: Before the median of grouped data can be computed, the raw class frequencies must be converted into a running total -- accumulating from the lowest class upward (less than type) or from the highest class downward (more than type) -- and then compared against half the total number of observations to find the one class (the median class) that contains the middle value.
concepts.rule: The cumulative frequency of a class is the sum of the frequencies of that class and all classes before it (less than type), or that class and all classes after it (more than type). To locate the median class, compute n/2 and find the first class (reading from the top) whose less-than-type cumulative frequency is greater than or equal to n/2.
concepts.example: For 53 students' marks (classes 0-10 through 90-100, frequencies 5, 3, 4, 3, 3, 4, 7, 9, 7, 8), the less-than-type cumulative frequencies are 5, 8, 12, 15, 18, 22, 29, 38, 45, 53; with n=53, n/2=26.5, and the first cumulative frequency reaching or passing 26.5 is 29 (class 60-70), so 60-70 is the median class (p. 190-193).

questions.q: A student argues: 'Since the modal class is the class with the highest frequency, and finding the median class also involves comparing frequencies, the median class and the modal class must always be the same class.' concepts.name: Median of Grouped Data: Formula and Applications
concepts.description: Computing the median of grouped data from the median class using the formula Median = l + ((n/2 - cf)/f) * h, including solving for an unknown frequency when the median is given.
concepts.idea: Once the median class is known, the median itself is pinned down by a formula that starts at the median class's lower limit and adds a fraction of the class width proportional to how far short the preceding cumulative frequency falls of half the total.
concepts.rule: Median = l + ((n/2 - cf)/f) * h, where l = lower limit of the median class, n = total number of observations, cf = cumulative frequency of the class preceding the median class, f = frequency of the median class, h = class size.

concepts.name: Comparing Mean, Median and Mode; the Empirical Relationship
concepts.description: Choosing the measure of central tendency (mean, median or mode) best suited to a given question or dataset, and using the approximate empirical relationship 3*Median = Mode + 2*Mean linking the three for a moderately skewed distribution.
concepts.idea: The three measures of central tendency answer different questions -- the mean uses every value and suits overall comparison, the median names a typical middle value that resists extreme scores, and the mode names the single most frequent value -- and for a moderately skewed distribution they are linked by an approximate empirical relationship, not three independent, unrelated numbers.
concepts.rule: The empirical relationship states 3 * Median = Mode + 2 * Mean (equivalently Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean, or Mean = (3*Median - Mode)/2). This is an approximation for a moderately skewed distribution, not an exact identity, so a value estimated from it may differ from the value obtained by direct computation.
concepts.example: For 30 students' marks data, mean=62 and mode=52 give an empirical estimate for the median of (52 + 2*62)/3 = 58.67, while the true median computed directly from the cumulative frequency table is 62.5 -- a visible gap that shows the relationship is only approximate (p. 183, p. 197).

questions.q: For 30 students' marks, the mean is 62 and the mode is 52. Use the empirical relationship to estimate the median.
questions.a: Using 3 * Median = Mode + 2 * Mean: 3 * Median = 52 + 2(62) = 52 + 124 = 176, so Median = 176/3 = 58.67 (approximately).

Correctly computes the estimated median as 58.67 (approximately)

questions.q: The true median of 30 students' marks data, computed directly from the cumulative frequency table (class intervals 10-25 through 85-100 with frequencies 2, 3, 7, 6, 6, 6), is 62.5. Compare this to the empirical estimate of 58.67 found from the mean (62) and mode (52), and state the size of the gap between them.
questions.a: The gap is 62.5 - 58.67 = 3.83 (approximately). The empirical estimate (58.67) is noticeably lower than the true median (62.5), confirming that the empirical relationship is only an approximation and can differ from the value obtained by direct computation.
s: Correctly computes the gap as approximately 3.83
Correctly concludes that the relationship is approximate and can genuinely differ from the true value

questions.q: For hospital patients' ages data (class intervals 5-15 through 55-65, step 10; frequencies 6, 11, 21, 23, 14, 5): the mean is 35.375 and the mode is 36.82 (approximately). (i) Use the empirical relationship to estimate the median. (ii) Separately, the true median computed directly from the cumulative frequency table works out to 35.87 (approximately). Compare the two values. (iii) Based on both this example and the 30-students'-marks example of this chapter (where the empirical estimate was 58.67 against a true median of 62.5), what general conclusion can you draw about how reliable the empirical relationship is?
questions.a: (i) 3 * Median = 36.82 + 2(35.375) = 36.82 + 70.75 = 107.57, Median = 107.57/3 = 35.86 (approximately). (ii) The empirical estimate (35.86) is extremely close to the true median (35.87) here, differing by only about 0.01. (iii) The empirical relationship can be very accurate for some distributions (as in this data) but noticeably off for others (as in the marks example, off by about 3.83); it is a useful quick approximation but not a reliable substitute for computing the median directly from the cumulative frequency table when precision matters.

questions.q: Consider these statements about comparing measures of central tendency. (II) The choice between mean, median and mode should depend on the specific question being asked and the nature of the data, such as whether extreme values are present. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: A company records the monthly salaries (in Rs) of its 20 employees. Nineteen earn between Rs 20,000 and Rs 30,000, while the owner earns Rs 500,000. (i) Explain what would happen to the mean salary if the owner's salary is included, compared to excluding it. (ii) State whether the median salary would be similarly affected by including the owner's salary. (iii) Recommend, with a reason, which measure (mean or median) better represents 'what a typical employee earns' here.
questions.a: (i) Including the owner's very high salary would pull the mean salary up sharply, far above what most employees actually earn. (ii) The median would be barely affected, since it depends only on the middle value(s) of the ordered data, and the owner's salary would simply become the single largest value at one end without shifting the middle. (iii) The median better represents a typical employee's earnings here, because it is not distorted by the one extreme value (the owner's salary), unlike the mean.
s: Correctly explains the mean would be pulled up sharply by the one extreme salary
Correctly explains the median would be barely affected
Correctly recommends the median with a valid reason tied to resistance to extreme values

questions.q: A student claims: 'Since 3 * Median = Mode + 2 * Mean is a proven formula, I can always use it to find the exact median instead of using the cumulative frequency formula, and save time.' Evaluate this claim, referring to the size of the gap seen in the 30-students'-marks example of this chapter (empirical estimate 58.67 versus true median 62.5).
questions.a: The claim is false. The relationship is an approximate empirical pattern observed for moderately skewed distributions, not a proven exact formula; the marks example itself shows a gap of about 3.83 between the empirical estimate (58.67) and the true median (62.5), which is large enough to matter in many practical situations. The cumulative-frequency-based median formula remains the reliable, exact method.
s: States the claim is false and correctly characterises the relationship as approximate, not an exact formula
Supports this using the actual gap from the marks example (about 3.83) as evidence

questions.q: Describe a real-life data collection scenario (different from any in this chapter) where you would expect the mean, median and mode to be noticeably different from one another, and explain in one line each why each of the three measures would behave the way you describe.
questions.a: Sample: the amount of money carried by 100 people walking through a train station. Most people carry small amounts (say Rs 100-500), while a few business travellers carry very large amounts (Rs 20,000 or more). Mean: pulled up well above what most people carry, because it is sensitive to the few very large amounts. Median: stays close to the typical small amount most people carry, since it depends only on the middle value. Mode: reflects the single most common amount carried (likely a small, round figure), which may be lower than or close to the median but well below the mean.
s: Gives a genuine, sensible real-life scenario likely to produce differing mean/median/mode
Correctly explains why the mean would differ (sensitivity to extreme/skewed values)
Correctly explains how the median and/or mode would behave differently from the mean, with valid reasoning
